cards.explanation: The reason God gives is that they are a rebellious house. He says it twice in one verse: “…for they are a rebellious house.” Their eyes and ears work fine, so the trouble isn't their equipment. I think that's what makes it sting. You can have perfect hearing and still not want to listen, and I know a few snooze buttons that prove it.

The trip is going into exile. God says, “…pack your bags for exile.” and later, “…go out like those who go into exile.” (Ezekiel 12:3-4). Exile means being forced away from home, so this is no vacation. Ezekiel is a man with a suitcase and a very serious message.

The answer is False. God doesn't say they are sure to understand. He says, “Perhaps they will understand, though they are a rebellious house.” “Perhaps” isn't “for sure,” and the verse keeps that difference. Ezekiel still packs the bags in full view, friends, and that's his job.

The answer is so he cannot see the land. God says, “cover your face so that you cannot see the land.” Ezekiel carries his bags out at dusk, and the covered face is part of the picture. Walking out with a blindfold-like cover on your face is a hard way to leave a place. Later God says the prince will do the very same thing (Ezekiel 12:12).

The word is sign. God says, “For I have made you a sign to the house of Israel.” A sign points at something beyond itself. Ezekiel's packing, wall digging and face covering are all pointing at what's coming for Jerusalem. He's the signpost, and the explanation comes the next morning.

The answer is True. The text says it right away: “So I did as I was commanded.” Ezekiel brings the bags out by day, digs through the wall in the evening and carries his things out at dusk. Digging through a wall by hand is not a normal evening, friends, and he did it anyway. That's obedience with dirt under the fingernails.

The burden concerns the prince in Jerusalem and the people there. God says, “This burden concerns the prince in Jerusalem and all the house of Israel who are there.” A burden here is a heavy message from the LORD. Ezekiel acts it out as they watch, but the message is about the prince and the people in Jerusalem.

The word is captives. God says, “they will go into exile as captives.” Ezekiel's act is a preview. “Just as it happened here, so will it be done to them…” Captives don't choose the trip, which makes it very different from packing for a vacation.

What God spreads over him is His net. God says, “…I will spread My net over him, and he will be caught in My snare.” The prince slips out of the city with his face covered, but he doesn't get away. A net is something you can't just walk out of. That's the picture God paints.

The answer is False. God says the prince will not see Babylon. He says, “I will bring him to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans; yet he will not see it, and there he will die.” The Chaldeans are the people who live in Babylon. It's a heavy verse, so I'll leave it quiet.

God spares a few so they can recount their abominations among the nations. He says He'll spare a few “…so that in the nations to which they go, they can recount all their abominations.” Then He adds, “Then they will know that I am the LORD.” So the few who are left will tell the story in the places they're scattered to. It's a small group carrying a big message.

God tells Ezekiel to eat his bread with trembling. He says, “…eat your bread with trembling, and drink your water with quivering and anxiety.” This time there's no wall and no bags. It's just a man at a meal, shaking. Even eating bread becomes part of the message.

The word is violence. God says the land “…will be stripped of everything in it because of the violence of all who dwell in it.” He names the reason Himself, and it's about how the people lived. I think it's a heavy verse, and I won't joke about the reason. The land is stripped because of what the people did.

The answer is False. God doesn't say the cities will stay standing. He says, “The inhabited cities will be laid waste, and the land will become desolate.” Cities and land go down together. Then He adds, “Then you will know that I am the LORD.”

When the people say every vision fails, they mean the visions never come true. The proverb says, “The days go by, and every vision fails…” which means time keeps passing and nothing happens. God answers it in the next verses, saying “…every vision will be fulfilled.” (Ezekiel 12:23). So He takes the claim head on.

The answer is True. God says, “I will put an end to this proverb, and in Israel they will no longer recite it.” He doesn't just argue with it, friends. He ends it. Then He tells Ezekiel to say, “The days are at hand when every vision will be fulfilled.”

The answer is True. God says, “For there will be no more false visions or flattering divinations within the house of Israel…” A flattering divination is a message that tells people what they want to hear. God says that kind is over. He puts it right next to His promise that His own word will be fulfilled.

The word is delay. God says, “…because I, the LORD, will speak whatever word I speak, and it will be fulfilled without delay.” Think of the proverb about the days going by and every vision failing. Here God says His word won't be held up. The people were saying it was taking forever, and this is the answer.

The answer is False. The saying is, “The vision that he sees is for many years from now; he prophesies about the distant future.” They're pushing it far away, which is different from saying it will never happen. God answers, “None of My words will be delayed any longer.”
